item.title: Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will hold ‘Christmases Not Forgotten’ for WWII survivors

item.content:encoded:
The Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will host Christmases Not Forgotten, a gathering honoring Guam’s World War II survivors who missed out on celebrating Christmas during the Japanese occupation.

The event is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Dec. 6 at the Zefiro Ballroom at LeoPalace Resort. It will bring together manåmko’ and their families for an afternoon of fellowship, music, dining, and honoring those whose lives were lost and those who survived WWII.

The Christmases Not Forgotten was created by a committee of the Mañenggon Memorial Foundation, including war survivor advisors Julia Villagomez, Rosa “Tan Chai” Duenas and David D.L. Flores. Foundation founders Willy Flores and Rita Franquez organized the gathering after hearing survivors share their experiences during and after the war. Flores said many survivors recalled missing family being together and gatherings of Christmas celebrations between 1941 and 1944.

Flores and Franquez said survivors recalled that during the war, some were able to say nobenas, or the CHamoru rosary, in secret.

“They could not get together openly, and they definitely could not celebrate Christmas,” Flores said. “They talked about how Christmas was taken from them in 1941, then of course 42, 43, and then 44. Even though the island was basically freed in July and August, still there was no time to put together Christmas in 44.”

The gathering will include live entertainment, a special surprise appearance, a visit from Santa Claus, gifts, and a shared meal. The foundation said their goal is to honor and celebrate the manåmko’ of Guam and those who have survived and lost their lives in WWII.

Admission is free for Guam WWII survivors. Individual tickets are $65. Family tables and corporate sponsorship opportunities are also available.

The foundation hopes the gathering will help preserve their stories and ensure future generations understand the experiences and sacrifices of those who lived through the war.

In a Nov. 18 letter to FinCEN acting Director Jenna Casanova, King-Hinds said federal investigations and prosecutions ove
item.content:encoded:
CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds has requested a briefing from the U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, to discuss concerns about illicit financial activity and the potential role of Chinese money laundering networks in the Commonwealth.

In a Nov. 18 letter to FinCEN acting Director Jenna Casanova, King-Hinds said federal investigations and prosecutions over the years have highlighted concerns about money laundering and other financial crimes linked to Chinese capital in the CNMI.

The delegate said more information is needed to understand how such networks operate, whether they remain active in the Northern Marianas and what steps federal and local officials can take to address potential risks.

King-Hinds requested a briefing with FinCEN officials to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by criminal organizations and to explore possible legislative, regulatory and enforcement measures to strengthen prevention efforts.

She said the CNMI's proximity to East Asia, its integration into the U.S. financial system and its economic ties to the region warrant closer examination of financial crime risks.

King-Hinds said protecting legitimate investment and economic activity while preventing illicit financial networks from exploiting local institutions is critical to the Commonwealth's economic and security interests.

item.content:encoded:
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has declared the day after Thanksgiving - Black Friday - a government of Guam holiday, giving government employees an additional day off this week

In an executive order issued Monday, Leon Guerrero designated Nov. 27 as a government holiday. All executive branch departments and agencies will be closed that day, with the exception of essential personnel and operations deemed necessary by agency heads to protect public health, safety and welfare.

The governor said the additional holiday recognizes the work of public servants while allowing families more time to spend together during the holiday season.

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio also encouraged residents to support local businesses over the extended holiday weekend and practice inafa’maolek by looking out for one another on the roads and in their neighborhoods.

Residents are encouraged to plan ahead for any government services they may need before the Friday closure.

item.title: EPA says initial tests show no toxic lead contamination in Iowa following detonation
item.description: Initial lab results from the controlled detonation of roughly five tons of unstable lead azide at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa showed no elevation of lead in water sources in the surrounding environment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday. "We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water sam
item.content:encoded:
Initial lab results from the controlled detonation of roughly five tons of unstable lead azide at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa showed no elevation of lead in water sources in the surrounding environment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday.

"We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples (collected pre and post detonation) rapidly return and get validated," the agency wrote in a post on X .

The EPA says a team of 300 personnel and contractors spent the days immediately following Wednesday's blast collecting samples, in addition to monitoring for airborne lead for 30 consecutive hours.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade or break down over time. It's especially dangerous to children and pregnant people, and experts say there is no safe level of exposure.

Military explosives experts detonated 68 drums of aging lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after it was found to be at risk of spontaneous explosion. Residents within five miles of the plant were ordered to evacuate, and many others told to stay inside, amid fears of a toxic plume of the chemicals.

In the hours immediately after the explosion, U.S. Army officials called the detonation a success, saying that the mitigation measures put in place – including layers of contaminant and downward-facing explosives meant to drive the blast into the ground – had "exceeded expectations."

Still, many residents and some elected officials have criticized the military for a lack of transparency in the operation, including Iowa Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who has called for an investigation into why the lead azide was allowed to get to this precarious point.

"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," he said after the detonation . "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared."

Sue Dyer, a corn and bean farmer about 18 miles southwest of the blast site, agreed that the biggest problem was communication, calling it "horrible."

"We didn't know anything about this until last week," she told NPR's Scott Simon in an interview on Saturday morning.

Dyer said that people in the community are all across the spectrum in terms of how worried they are after the detonation, even with reassurances from the federal government.

"Some people are sure that we're absolutely fine, and some people think we're absolutely dead. So put me somewhere in the middle until I have the data to make an opinion," she said, noting she is waiting for independent sampling results as well as those from the EPA.

Dyer says she had samples taken from her farmland before the blast and plans on taking her own samples again in the coming days, in hopes to get her farm verified lead-free.

"But what do you do if there's lead there?" Dyer asked. "I'm very hopeful that everything's fine, but I'm also a realist."

item.title: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 10, wounds 110
item.description: Updated November 29, 2026 at 1:04 AM ChST KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a primary and middle school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed 10 people and wounded another 110, most of them children, officials said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 29, 2026 at 1:04 AM ChST

KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a primary and middle school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed 10 people and wounded another 110, most of them children, officials said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Kunar Culture and Information Director Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.

Interior ministry spokesman Abdul Mateen Qani put the death toll at 10, and said 110 had been wounded.

Footage from a ward in the hospital showed young children, several with bandaged heads and some lying two to a bed.

Noor Rahman, whose home is next door to the school, said he heard the explosion and saw dust rising.

"I ran straight into the dust, our own children were there," he said. "I entered one of the rooms, where there was screaming and shouting. I saw the hand of my niece, she was moving it. I rushed in, cleared away the bricks, and managed to pull her out, along with other injured (people)."

Haji Sulaiman, whose son was wounded in the blast, said he had been on his way to his shop when he heard and saw the explosion.

"Pieces of wood and human flesh were flying everywhere," said Sulaiman, adding that he ran toward the school. "When I arrived, I found children, some were dead, others were drenched in blood, and some rooftops were collapsed, the walls were gone, and nothing remained of the school."

Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.

Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.

In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

item.title: New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
item.description: The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer. Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor
item.content:encoded:
The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.

Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.

The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.

And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.

"Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.

Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.

"There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.

In an interview with NPR, Piper contended that Republican attorneys generals' policies are still broadly supported by voters, but were overshadowed by the unpopularity of the rest of the GOP. He noted that Republican attorneys general candidates ran ahead of GOP candidates for governor and U.S. Senate in some states.

Following the midterm results, Republican attorneys general convened for their fall meeting in Dallas, Texas, where the outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, lost his bid for Senate. He will soon be replaced by a Democrat, Nathan Johnson.

Piper said attendees grimly reflected on their challenges while also strategizing how to position Republican attorneys general to support the GOP as 2028 approaches. He added that the Republican Attorneys General Association are watching for potential "lawfare" by Democrats, including changing the number of Supreme Court justices or welcoming new states into the Union.

"We have to have better quality of candidates at the top of the ticket," Piper said. "We have to have better message discipline, and we need other committees in Washington to focus on what RAGA has done, and that is making sure we're good stewards of resources."

Democratic attorneys general held their own conference in Chicago, which some attendees said was both a celebration of the Democratic victories and an orientation for the incoming Democratic attorneys general.

"While a lot of the focus turns to what's next in Washington, we understand and we're not naive to the fact that we will continue to have a critical role in protecting our republic," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul during a Nov. 19 press briefing with other Democratic attorneys general.

Johnson, the incoming Texas attorney general, said at the same briefing that the wins for Democrats in the state house and governor's mansion could prompt Republicans to cooperate on a "cleansing" anti-corruption agenda. But he also signaled he'd support legislation and legal challenges to President Donald Trump's efforts to build a wall in Big Bend National Park on Texas' border with Mexico.

The Texas attorney general has traditionally brought cases on behalf conservative legal causes that had wide-ranging impacts across the country. The office also served as a training ground for Republican legal talent. U.S. Sen. John Cornyn and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott both served as attorney general before seeking higher office, while Sen. Ted Cruz served as solicitor general in the office before running for Congress. Other staffers have gone on to serve as judges, law clerks and prosecutors.

"Texas was a major intellectual force for the Republican attorneys general, and that's not going to be easily replaced," said James Tierney, a professor at Harvard Law School who has advised more than thirty attorneys general from both parties on staffing and legal philosophy.

"There are a lot of very smart, good lawyers in various AG offices who are very conservative," said Tierney. "But they don't have the heft and the size and the number of attorneys that Texas brings, and so for them, it's a very significant loss."

For Democrats, the recent wins could transform how the states enforce laws, bring legal cases, and support or hinder the Trump administration.

"These new attorneys general are not going to be particularly favorable towards the Trump administration, and will take an oppositional position in a number of different cases," said Anthony Michael Kreis, a constitutional law professor at Georgia State University. That may mean direct lawsuits against the administration in coalition with other attorneys general, Kreis said.

Many incoming Democratic attorneys general campaigned on bringing cases against alleged price gouging and digital surveillance by companies, as well as a tougher approach to antitrust concerns. But they will also face pressure to listen to their local business communities–including major multinational corporations.

"I think it's actually likely to increase bipartisan coalitions, particularly on economic issues," said Swain Wood, a partner at the law firm WilmerHale who now co-chairs the firm's practice advising clients on state attorneys general. Wood, who served as assistant attorney general to North Carolina Democratic Attorney General Josh Stein, cited past landmark settlements against tobacco and opioid distributors as cases where bipartisan groups of attorneys general found common ground.

Attorneys general from both parties have also banded together in recent years on cases about regulating social media platforms . Democrats elected in newly-minted swing states may already face pressure to choose popular or bipartisan legal actions. That's one way to maintain voters' support, as they're likely to face stiff reelection challenges.

item.title: 17 films to see before New Year's, from Oscar-bait to blockbusters
item.description: Hollywood's heading into the holidays on a high note. Odysseus and Spider-Man led cinemas to the biggest summer ever at the box office. Since then, studio hits have been jockeying with indie surprises like You Can See Everything . In theaters this Thanksgiving are Focker-in-Law , Club Kid , the Rocky origin story , another unforgettable Andrew Scott performance , a Hunger Games sequel and more. Bu
item.content:encoded:
Hollywood's heading into the holidays on a high note. Odysseus and Spider-Man led cinemas to the biggest summer ever at the box office. Since then, studio hits have been jockeying with indie surprises like You Can See Everything . In theaters this Thanksgiving are Focker-in-Law , Club Kid , the Rocky origin story , another unforgettable Andrew Scott performance , a Hunger Games sequel and more.

But Tinseltown may have saved the best — or at least the buzziest — for last. Here's what else is coming between now and year's end.

Pedro Pascal spent months practicing cello many hours a day so he'd look convincing playing a cello in the fictional drama Behemoth! , about a musician whose personal life gets in the way of his art.

Artistic temperaments are in comic opposition in The Gallerist , in which struggling art gallery owner Natalie Portman spars with art influencer Zach Galifianakis, who clearly has it in for her. When he accidentally trips and skewers himself on a very sharp sculpture —and dies just before the gallery's public opening — she decides she has little choice but to try to pass him off as conceptual art.

In Los Angeles and New York starting on Dec. 4

In 1968, Jane Elliott came up with a classroom exercise to help elementary school kids understand the unfairness of racism: "blue-eyed people are better than brown-eyed people," she told the kids. For that lesson, she got both fame and hate mail. In the documentary Jane Elliott Against the World , she's still going strong, sharing the lessons she learned back then. The film will also be shown on PBS Independent Lens on March 29, 2027.

In New York starting Dec. 4, expands in January

The title of the jazzy bio-pic Everybody Digs Bill Evans certainly qualifies as truth-in-advertising: Evans (Anders Danielsen Lie) had a difficult life, but he made glorious music. Laurie Metcalf and Bill Pullman play his folks.

Never-released footage of the singer-songwriter George Michael led to this concert film, captured over two nights in Paris in 1988 on his first headlining solo tour.

In Los Angeles and New York on Dec. 11, then expanding in December and into January

During the workday, the social workers in Tender Loving Care face clients who claim they don't need any help; when they're off the clock, it's aging family members. 83-year-old filmmaker Mike Leigh says Tender Loving Care will be his final film, and a lovely, elegiac one it is.

In theaters Dec. 11 and on Netflix Jan. 8

This journalism saga charts the 1960s rise of news mogul Rupert Murdoch, played here by a brash Guy Pearce, who altered Britain's staid news landscape when he bought a London tabloid. Jack O'Connell plays The Sun editor Larry Lamb, Claire Foy a reporter, and director Danny Boyle tells the story with tabloid-esque flair.

In Jesse Eisenberg's warmly funny comedy, Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti play, respectively, a timid housewife who tries out for a musical ("I haven't sung in front of anyone since church choir") and the tyrannical director who's the self-styled "biggest name in New Jersey community theater." Watching Moore pretend to be a bad actor is fascinating.

Sandra Hüller disguises herself as a man to fight in a 17th century war, then continues to live as a man so she can inherit a neglected country estate, even though that means she must marry and somehow hide her true identity from her wife.

In an unprecedented battle-of-the-blockbusters that industry-watchers are calling "Dunes-Day," Marvel's superhero showdown opens on the same day as the sci-fi spectacle Dune: Part Three . With Dune having locked down every single IMAX theater for the first three weeks, Marvel has rebranded other premium-format screens so that the Avengers can play in what the company is calling " Infinity Vision ."

The finale to Denis Villeneuve's intergalactic trilogy corresponds roughly with Frank Herbert's second novel, Dune Messiah , in which Muad'Dib (Timothée Chalamet) realizes that after years of war, he's become the oppressor that Chani (Zendaya) is fighting.

In New York and Los Angeles Dec. 18 for one week, opens again in theaters in January

Taking stabs at the patriarchy in a serious way is Sophie Okonedo in this ruminative drama, which transplants Virginia Woolf's feminist novel Mrs. Dalloway t o contemporary Nigeria. Ayo Edebiri and David Oyelowo offer support.

In limited theaters Dec. 25, everywhere Jan. 8

Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino has Andrew Garfield play Open AI creator Sam Altman as a kind of seductive vampire of a tech-bro in a film that will not reassure anybody about the future of AI. It explores what happened when tech guys who'd said they wanted to keep the world safe from artificial intelligence decided they'd just as soon make money off it.

Director Robert Eggers, who recently gave us a gothic-horror vampire in Nosferatu , brings another supernatural critter to life in this black-and-white art film. Aaron Taylor-Johnson sprouts fangs, Willem Dafoe's the huntsman.

In this family-oriented sequel, instead of players getting pulled into the Jumanji game, critters from the game escape into the real world. So do some mixed-up avatars. This time, Spencer's mother Janice takes the form of Dwayne Johnson's Dr. Smolder Bravestone, and Kevin Hart embodies 7-year-old Tyson ("except I'm a Black grownup").

Two closeted gay men find each other in Lukas Dhont's World War I battlefield epic, ironically titled Coward . Just to survive, these guys have to be brave on quite a few fronts.

The final pick of the NFL draft in 1983, John Tuggle (played by sometime-Superman David Corenswet) defied the odds to land a starting spot on the New York Giants. Did a subsequent cancer diagnosis slow him down? "If I'm not the guy who keeps on fighting," he says in the film, "I don't know who I am."
